America and the War on Terror

options.text: The Taliban government in Afghanistan sheltered al-Qaeda, the network behind the attacks
Afghanistan had invaded the United States in the summer of 2001
options.misconception: Afghanistan never invaded the United States.

options.text: Iraq had already surrendered to the United States in 2000
options.misconception: Iraq had not surrendered; the United States invaded Iraq in 2003.

options.text: The United Nations ordered the United States to attack Afghanistan first
options.misconception: The United States chose Afghanistan; no United Nations order set the order.

rationales.A: Background: al-Qaeda operated under the protection of the Taliban government in Afghanistan, so the first campaign aimed to remove that shelter.
rationales.B: No Afghan force attacked the United States. The attacks were carried out by hijackers linked to al-Qaeda.
rationales.C: Background: Iraq had not surrendered, and the United States invaded Iraq in March 2003, after the Afghanistan campaign began.
rationales.D: Background: the United States acted with allies in Afghanistan, but the choice of Afghanistan came from where al-Qaeda was based, not from a United Nations order.
rationales.general:
1. Ask where the attackers were based. The account links the hijackers to al-Qaeda.
2. Background: al-Qaeda operated under the protection of the Taliban government in Afghanistan.
3. That made Afghanistan the first target: removing the shelter came before any wider campaign.
4. Background: Iraq entered the picture later, in 2003, on a different claim about weapons.
Remember: a first response aims at where the attackers were sheltered.

stem: Why did the United States launch its first military response to the September 11 attacks in Afghanistan rather than in Iraq?

stimulus.source_note: Photograph by the U.S. Air Force, September 11, 2001, Arlington, Virginia. Public domain (U.S. federal government work). Account paraphrased from the grounding books (Barron's Premium 2027 Ch. 11, Topic 9.6; 5 Steps 2024 Ch. 30).
stimulus.text:
Photograph of the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, after the September 11, 2001 attacks: one wing is a burned-out ruin, cranes and fire trucks work around the wreckage, and a large American flag hangs from the part of the building still standing.

Paraphrase of a secondary account: On the morning of September 11, 2001, nineteen hijackers linked to the al-Qaeda network seized four passenger planes. Two planes struck the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York City, one struck the Pentagon, and a fourth crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought the hijackers. Nearly 3,000 people were killed.
